newsitem.title: USA: U.S. presses for ouster of Bosnian official.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presses for ouster of Bosnian official.

text.p: U.S. arms shipped to former Yugoslavia will only be handed over to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation once a Bosnian official seen as close to Iran has resigned, administration officials said on Thursday.

The officials made clear the tanks, guns and helicopters, which arrived on Thursday in the Croatian port of Ploce, would stay under U.S. control until Bosnia's government took several steps, including ousting Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic.
This could happen within the next few days, said one official, speaking on condition he was not identified.

The weaponry that arrived in Ploce aboard a chartered ship comprised the bulk of a $100 million shipment for the Federation under a U.S. "train-and-equip" programme designed to make the Moslems and Croats a match for the Bosnian Serbs.

Unloading was to begin on Friday and last two to three days, a U.S. official at the scene said. Officials said the arms would then be transported overland to storage sites in Bosnia approved by the international peace force there, IFOR.

But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the equipment "will only be shipped to those storage sites when some remaining issues of concern to the United States are resolved on a satisfactory basis by the Bosnian government."

"These issues relate to the implementation of key components of the Federation defence law and some additional steps needed to promote cooperation in forming the joint armed forces in the Federation," he added.
The defence law, passed under U.S. pressure earlier this year, aims to merge gradually the previously separate forces of the Moslems and Croats.
Burns declined to identify the issues at stake. But a senior administration official said Washington was concerned about a particular Bosnian Defence Ministry official.

"We think he cannot play a useful role in coordinating with us on this programme, so we've asked for him to step down ... and I think in a couple of days he will," he said. Asked if it was the deputy defence minister, the official said: "That's a good guess."

Cengic himself said in Sarajevo on Oct. 8 that the United States was pushing for his removal, after the Washington Post reported he was trying to block the train-and-equip programme and had close ties to Iran.

The U.S. official said there were also other issues involved concerning the defence law. But he said: "The bar is not high. There are things that can be done and can be done quickly, and then this equipment will be delivered."

The U.S. equipment includes 45 M-60 battle tanks, 80 M-11 armoured personnel carriers, 15 UH-1H helicopters, 840 light anti-tank weapons, 45,000 M-16 rifles and ammunition. The programme also includes instruction for Federation army troops.

European powers have criticised Washington's patronage of Moslem-Croat forces, saying it undermined diplomatic goals to promote reconciliation and arms control in Bosnia, divided by the Dayton peace accord into the Federation and a Serb entity.

The Moslem-led Bosnian army was outgunned by Serb forces during a 43-month war in the Balkan republic and had to rely on Islamic countries such as Iran for arms shipments, which violated an international arms embargo on former Yugoslavia.
In August, the United States sent a symbolic advance shipment of 1,000 rifles, 200 machine guns, associated ammunition and 200 tactical radios.
Instruction of Bosnian soldiers began this month when a team of 170 retired U.S. officers from the private firm MPRI, based in Alexandria, Virginia, launched a training programme near Sarajevo.
